decks.title: Work, Energy and Power — Part 1: Work, units and power
goals: Calculate work done using W = F s cos θ
Explain when no work is done
Convert between joule, erg, calorie, kilowatt hour and electron volt
Calculate power and convert between watt and horsepower

slides.heading: Hard work or no work?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — in physics, work is done only when a force moves its point of application. Holding a heavy bag still may tire you, but it does no work on the bag.

rows: Lifting a bucket from a well
Holding a bag still at shoulder height
Carrying a bag along a level corridor
Pushing a stalled car that moves 5 m

visual.alt: Table of four everyday situations and whether work is done

slides.narration: Namaste! In everyday speech, work means effort. In physics, work is done only when a force makes something move in the direction of the force. Holding a heavy bag still tires your arms, but because the bag does not move, no work is done on it. In this part we learn to calculate work, energy and power.

slides.heading: Work done by a force
slides.body_md: **Work** is done when a force displaces a body: $W = F\,s\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the force and the displacement. Only the component $F\cos\theta$ along the displacement does work. **Special cases:** $\theta = 0^\circ$: $W = Fs$ (maximum); $\theta = 90^\circ$: $W = 0$ (a coolie carrying a load on his head across a level platform does no work against gravity); $\theta = 180^\circ$: $W = -Fs$ (friction does negative work). **Work against gravity:** lifting a mass $m$ through height $h$: $W = mgh$. Work is a scalar.

visual.alt: A box pulled by a force at an angle, resolved into a horizontal component that does work and a vertical component that does none

slides.narration: Work equals the force times the displacement times the cosine of the angle between them. Only the part of the force along the motion does work. If the force is along the motion, the work is simply force times distance. If the force is at right angles to the motion, no work is done. And when you lift a mass, the work done against gravity is mass times g times height.

slides.heading: Worked example: pulling at an angle
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A child pulls a toy cart 8 m along the floor with a force of 15 N along a string at $60^\circ$ to the floor. Find the work done. How much work would the same force do if the string were horizontal?

**At $60^\circ$:** $W = F s \cos\theta = 15 \times 8 \times \cos 60^\circ = 15 \times 8 \times 0.5 = 60\ \text{J}$.

**Horizontal:** $W = 15 \times 8 = 120\ \text{J}$ — the pull at an angle wastes part of the force lifting rather than moving the cart.

visual.alt: Table of work done by a 15 newton force over 8 metres at three angles

slides.narration: Only the part of the pull along the floor does work. At sixty degrees that part is half the force, so the work is fifteen times eight times one half, which is sixty joules. With the string flat along the floor, the whole force acts along the motion and the work doubles to a hundred and twenty joules.

slides.heading: Quick check: work
slides.body_md: Decide whether, and how much, work is done.
slides.narration: Quick check. Work needs a displacement with a component along the force.

slides.heading: Energy and its units
slides.body_md: **Energy** is the capacity to do work; it is measured in the same units as work. **Joule (J):** work done when a force of 1 N moves its point of application 1 m along the force. **Erg** (cgs): 1 dyne × 1 cm; $1\ \text{J} = 10^{7}\ \text{erg}$. **Calorie:** $1\ \text{cal} \approx 4.2\ \text{J}$. **Kilowatt hour (kW h):** energy used by a 1 kW device in 1 h; $1\ \text{kW h} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}$. **Electron volt (eV):** energy gained by an electron through 1 V; $1\ \text{eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$.

visual.alt: Table of units of energy with their values in joules and typical uses

slides.narration: Energy is the ability to do work, so it has the same units as work. The joule is the SI unit. Smaller units include the erg, a ten millionth of a joule, and the electron volt, used for atoms. Larger units include the calorie for heat and the kilowatt hour, which appears on electricity bills and equals three point six million joules.

slides.heading: Worked example: converting units
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Convert (a) 2.5 kW h into joules, (b) 840 J into calories, and (c) 0.3 J into ergs.

**(a)** $2.5 \times 3.6 \times 10^{6} = 9 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}$.

**(b)** $840 \div 4.2 = 200\ \text{cal}$.

**(c)** $0.3 \times 10^{7} = 3 \times 10^{6}\ \text{erg}$.

visual.alt: Flow of conversion factors from kilowatt hours to joules and from joules to ergs and calories

slides.narration: Always go through joules. Two and a half kilowatt hours is two and a half times three point six million, which is nine million joules. Eight hundred and forty joules divided by four point two gives two hundred calories. And nought point three joules times ten million gives three million ergs.

slides.heading: Quick check: units of energy
slides.body_md: Convert between units of energy.
slides.narration: Quick check. One kilowatt hour is three point six million joules.

slides.heading: Power
slides.body_md: **Power** is the rate of doing work: $P = \dfrac{W}{t}$. SI unit: **watt (W)** = 1 J s⁻¹. Bigger units: $1\ \text{kW} = 10^{3}\ \text{W}$, $1\ \text{MW} = 10^{6}\ \text{W}$, $1\ \text{GW} = 10^{9}\ \text{W}$. **Horsepower:** $1\ \text{hp} = 746\ \text{W}$. **Energy vs power:** two students of equal weight climbing the same stairs do the same work (gain the same energy), but the one who climbs faster has more power.

visual.alt: Table comparing work, energy and power and their units

slides.narration: Power tells us how quickly work is done. It equals work divided by time and is measured in watts, where one watt is one joule per second. Engines are sometimes rated in horsepower, which is seven hundred and forty six watts. Two equal-weight students climbing the same stairs do the same work, but the faster one develops more power.

slides.heading: Worked example: climbing stairs
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Riya (mass 50 kg) climbs 30 steps, each 0.2 m high, in 15 s. Take $g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Find (a) the work done against gravity, (b) her power, and (c) her power in horsepower.

**(a)** $h = 30 \times 0.2 = 6\ \text{m}$; $W = mgh = 50 \times 10 \times 6 = 3000\ \text{J}$.

**(b)** $P = W/t = 3000 \div 15 = 200\ \text{W}$.

**(c)** $200 \div 746 = 0.27\ \text{hp}$.

visual.alt: Table of the stair-climbing results

slides.narration: Thirty steps of nought point two metres take Riya six metres up. The work against gravity is her mass times g times height: fifty times ten times six, which is three thousand joules. Doing this in fifteen seconds means a power of two hundred watts, a little over a quarter of a horsepower.

slides.heading: Quick check: power
slides.body_md: Calculate or compare power.
slides.narration: Quick check. Power is work divided by time.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: W = F s cos θ; W = 0 when θ = 90°; W = mgh against gravity.
Energy = capacity to do work; units J, erg, cal, kW h, eV.
P = W/t; 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹; 1 hp = 746 W.

visual.alt: Summary table of formulae in Part 1

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Work equals force times displacement times the cosine of the angle between them, and no work is done when they are at right angles. Energy is the ability to do work and has several units, all convertible to joules. Power is the rate of doing work, measured in watts.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Write the formula, substitute with units, then give the answer with its unit.
Convert grams to kilograms and centimetres to metres first.
kW h is a unit of energy, not power.
For “no work done”, give the reason: zero displacement or force perpendicular to displacement.

rows: kW h is a unit of power
It is a unit of energy
Work = F × s at any angle

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. In every calculation, write the formula, substitute with units and give the unit of the answer. Change grams to kilograms and centimetres to metres first. Remember that the kilowatt hour measures energy, not power. And when no work is done, say why: either nothing moved, or the force was at right angles to the motion.

decks.title: Work, Energy and Power — Part 2: Mechanical energy and its conservation
goals: Derive U = mgh and K = ½mv²
Solve problems on potential and kinetic energy
Identify energy conversions in everyday devices
Show that U + K is constant for a freely falling body and describe a pendulum’s energy changes

slides.heading: Stored and moving energy
slides.body_md: Part 2 — a raised hammer stores energy because of its position; a moving hammer has energy because of its motion. Energy changes form, but the total stays the same.

rows: A wound spring of a toy car

visual.alt: Table of four objects and their main form of mechanical energy

slides.narration: Water held high behind a dam can turn turbines when released; it has energy because of its position. A cricket ball flying through the air has energy because of its motion. In this part we calculate these two forms of mechanical energy and see that, as one turns into the other, the total stays constant.

slides.heading: Potential energy: U = mgh
slides.body_md: **Potential energy** is the energy a body has because of its **position or configuration** (a raised stone, a stretched bow). **Gravitational potential energy** of a mass $m$ at height $h$: the work done to raise it against its weight $mg$ is $W = F \times s = mg \times h$, and this work is stored, so $U = mgh$. It is measured from a chosen reference level (usually the ground).

visual.alt: Table of three masses at different heights and their gravitational potential energies

slides.narration: Potential energy is energy stored because of position or shape, like a raised stone or a stretched bow. To lift a mass through a height, you must push up with a force equal to its weight, mass times g, through that height. The work done, mass times g times height, is stored as gravitational potential energy.

slides.heading: Kinetic energy: K = ½mv²
slides.body_md: **Kinetic energy** is the energy of a body **due to its motion**. **Derivation:** a force $F$ accelerates a mass $m$ from rest to speed $v$ over distance $s$. From $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as$ with $u = 0$: $s = \dfrac{v^{2}}{2a}$. Work done $W = F s = ma \times \dfrac{v^{2}}{2a} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$, stored as $K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$. Doubling $v$ makes $K$ four times as large. Forms: **translational** (moving along), **rotational** (spinning wheel), **vibrational** (atoms in a solid).

visual.alt: Table of how kinetic energy changes when mass or speed changes

slides.narration: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. If a steady force speeds a mass up from rest, the work it does turns out to be half times mass times speed squared, and this becomes the kinetic energy. Because speed is squared, doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times larger. A body can move along, spin or vibrate, giving three forms of kinetic energy.

slides.heading: Worked example: potential and kinetic energy
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A 0.15 kg cricket ball is thrown at 20 m s⁻¹. (a) Find its kinetic energy. (b) How much would its kinetic energy be at 10 m s⁻¹? (c) To what height could this kinetic energy (at 20 m s⁻¹) raise the ball if it all became potential energy? ($g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$)

**(a)** $K = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.15 \times 20^{2} = 30\ \text{J}$.

**(b)** Speed halved, so $K = 30 \div 4 = 7.5\ \text{J}$.

**(c)** $mgh = 30$, so $h = 30 \div (0.15 \times 10) = 20\ \text{m}$.

visual.alt: Table of the cricket ball results

slides.narration: Half times nought point one five times twenty squared gives thirty joules of kinetic energy. At half the speed the kinetic energy is a quarter, seven and a half joules. If all thirty joules became potential energy, the ball could rise until mass times g times height equals thirty, which is twenty metres.

slides.heading: Quick check: kinetic energy
slides.body_md: Predict how kinetic energy changes.
slides.narration: Quick check. Kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed.

slides.heading: Other forms of energy and conversions
slides.body_md: Besides mechanical energy there are **heat, light, sound, chemical, electrical, nuclear** and **magnetic** energy. Devices **convert** energy from one form to another; some is always wasted, usually as heat.

visual.alt: Table of six devices with their input and useful output energy

slides.narration: Energy comes in many forms: heat, light, sound, chemical, electrical and nuclear, besides mechanical. Devices change energy from one form to another. A battery turns chemical energy into electrical energy; a loudspeaker turns electrical energy into sound; a solar cell turns light into electrical energy; and a heater turns electrical energy into heat.

slides.heading: Worked example: tracing energy changes
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Trace the energy changes in (a) a hydroelectric power station, (b) a torch, and (c) a person climbing stairs after eating.

**(a)** Potential energy of stored water → kinetic energy of falling water → kinetic energy of turbine → electrical energy.

**(b)** Chemical (cells) → electrical → light (and some heat).

**(c)** Chemical (food) → mechanical (muscles) → potential energy of the body (and heat).

visual.alt: Flow of energy changes in a hydroelectric power station

slides.narration: Follow the energy step by step. Water stored high in a dam has potential energy, which becomes kinetic energy as it falls, spins the turbine, and is turned into electrical energy by the generator. In a torch, chemical energy in the cells becomes electrical energy and then light. When you climb stairs, energy from food is turned into potential energy of your body.

slides.heading: Quick check: energy conversions
slides.body_md: Identify the energy change in a device.
slides.narration: Quick check. Ask what form goes in and what useful form comes out.

slides.heading: Conservation of energy; free fall
slides.body_md: **Principle of conservation of energy:** energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only change from one form to another, and the total energy of an isolated system stays constant. **Free fall** (air resistance neglected): as a body falls, $U$ decreases and $K$ increases by the same amount, so $U + K = mgH$ at every height. A 2 kg ball dropped from 20 m: total $= 400\ \text{J}$ throughout.

visual.alt: Energy of a 2 kilogram ball falling from 20 metres against height: potential energy falls in a straight line from 400 joules at the top to zero at the ground, kinetic energy rises from zero to 400 joules, and their total stays at 400 joules
visual.caption: U + K = 400 J at every height (air resistance neglected).

slides.narration: Energy cannot be made or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. For a falling ball, potential energy is lost and exactly the same amount of kinetic energy is gained. So the total stays the same at every height. A two kilogram ball dropped from twenty metres has four hundred joules at the top, all potential, and four hundred joules just before landing, all kinetic.

slides.heading: Worked example: energy at three heights
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A 2 kg ball is dropped from 20 m ($g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$). Find $U$, $K$ and $U + K$ (a) at the top, (b) after falling 5 m, (c) just before it hits the ground, and its speed at (c).

**(a)** $U = 2 \times 10 \times 20 = 400\ \text{J}$, $K = 0$; total 400 J.

**(b)** $h = 15\ \text{m}$: $U = 300\ \text{J}$; $v^{2} = 2 \times 10 \times 5 = 100$, $K = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 100 = 100\ \text{J}$; total 400 J.

**(c)** $U = 0$, $K = 400\ \text{J}$; $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times v^{2} = 400$, so $v = 20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Table of potential, kinetic and total energy of the falling ball at three heights

slides.narration: At the top the ball has four hundred joules, all potential. After falling five metres it is at fifteen metres, with three hundred joules of potential energy; its speed squared is a hundred, so it has a hundred joules of kinetic energy. The total is still four hundred. Just before landing all four hundred joules are kinetic, so the speed is twenty metres per second.

slides.heading: The simple pendulum
slides.body_md: In a swinging pendulum, at the **extreme positions** the bob is momentarily at rest at its highest point: energy is **all potential**. At the **mean position** it is lowest and fastest: energy is **all kinetic**. In between it is partly each. The total stays constant; in practice air resistance slowly converts it to heat, so the swings die away.

visual.alt: A simple pendulum with all potential energy at the two extreme positions and all kinetic energy at the mean position

slides.narration: A pendulum shows energy changing back and forth. At either end of its swing, the bob stops for an instant at its highest point, so all its energy is potential. At the middle it is lowest and moving fastest, so all its energy is kinetic. In a real pendulum, air resistance slowly turns the energy into heat, and the swings get smaller.

slides.heading: Quick check: conservation of energy
slides.body_md: Apply conservation of mechanical energy.
slides.narration: Quick check. Potential energy lost equals kinetic energy gained.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: U = mgh (energy of position); K = ½mv² (energy of motion); both derived from W = F s.
Devices convert energy; some is always lost as heat.
Conservation of energy: total constant; for free fall U + K = mgH.
Pendulum: all PE at the extremes, all KE at the mean position.

visual.alt: Summary table of formulae in Part 2

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Potential energy, mass times g times height, depends on position; kinetic energy, half mass times speed squared, depends on motion. Devices change energy from one form to another. The total energy is always conserved, so for a falling body potential plus kinetic energy stays constant, and a pendulum trades one for the other.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Square the speed before multiplying in K = ½mv².
For “speed on reaching the ground”, use mgh = ½mv² — the mass cancels.
In derivations, state the starting formula (W = F s) and the equation of motion used.
Only translational K and U are examined numerically.

rows: Total energy rises as the ball falls

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 2 and their fixes

slides.narration: Final tips. Always square the speed in the kinetic energy formula. To find the speed of a falling body at the ground, equate mass times g times height to half mass times speed squared; the mass cancels. In derivations, show which equation you start from. And remember that only translational kinetic and potential energy are asked in numericals.

notes.title: Work, Energy and Power — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Work
sections.body_md:
Work is done when a force moves its point of application: $W = F s \cos\theta$ ($\theta$ = angle between force and displacement). Scalar; SI unit joule.

- $\theta = 0^\circ$: $W = Fs$. $\theta = 90^\circ$: $W = 0$ (load carried horizontally; a satellite in circular orbit). $\theta = 180^\circ$: $W = -Fs$ (friction, braking).
- Work against gravity in lifting mass $m$ through height $h$: $W = mgh$.

key_terms.definition_md: The product of a force and the displacement of its point of application in the direction of the force.
The work done when a force of one newton moves its point of application one metre in its own direction.

formulas.label: Work by a force at an angle

visual.alt: Table of work done at three angles

sections.heading: 2. Energy and its units
sections.body_md:
Energy: the capacity to do work; same units as work.

| Unit | Value |
|---|---|
| 1 J | $10^{7}$ erg |
| 1 calorie | ≈ 4.2 J |
| 1 kW h | $3.6 \times 10^{6}$ J |
| 1 eV | $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ J |

key_terms.definition_md: The capacity of a body to do work.
The energy used by a one-kilowatt device in one hour, equal to 3.6 million joules.

visual.alt: Table of conversion factors

sections.heading: 3. Power
sections.body_md:
Power = rate of doing work: $P = \dfrac{W}{t}$. SI unit watt (1 J s⁻¹); kW = $10^{3}$ W, MW = $10^{6}$ W, GW = $10^{9}$ W; **1 hp = 746 W**.

Energy (how much work) differs from power (how fast): equal-weight students climbing the same stairs gain the same energy; the faster one has more power.

key_terms.definition_md: The rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.
The power of a device that does one joule of work per second.

visual.alt: Table of power units in watts

sections.heading: 4. Potential and kinetic energy
sections.body_md:
**Gravitational potential energy:** work done to raise $m$ through $h$ against $mg$: $U = mgh$.

**Kinetic energy:** a force $F$ accelerates $m$ from rest; $v^{2} = 2as$, so $W = Fs = ma \cdot \dfrac{v^{2}}{2a} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$: $K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$.

Kinetic energy may be translational, rotational or vibrational (only translational is examined numerically). Doubling $v$ quadruples $K$.

key_terms.definition_md: Energy possessed by a body because of its position or configuration.
Energy possessed by a body because of its motion.

visual.alt: Table of how kinetic energy scales with speed

sections.heading: 5. Other forms of energy and conversions
sections.body_md:
Forms: mechanical, heat, light, sound, chemical, electrical, magnetic, nuclear.

| Device | Conversion |
|---|---|
| Cell | Chemical → electrical |
| Loudspeaker | Electrical → sound |
| Microphone | Sound → electrical |
| Solar cell | Light → electrical |
| Electric heater | Electrical → heat |
| Steam engine | Heat → mechanical |

key_terms.definition_md: The change of energy from one form to another, as in a device.

visual.alt: Table of three devices and their useful output

sections.heading: 6. Conservation of energy
sections.body_md:
**Principle:** energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it changes form, and the total energy of an isolated system is constant.

**Free fall** from height $H$ (no air resistance): at any height $h$, $U = mgh$ and $K = mg(H - h)$, so $U + K = mgH$. Speed at the ground: $v = \sqrt{2gH}$.

**Simple pendulum:** all PE at the extremes, all KE at the mean position; total constant (air resistance slowly turns it into heat).

key_terms.definition_md: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only change from one form to another.

visual.alt: Table of energy at pendulum positions

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Forgetting cos θ when the force is at an angle.
- Treating kW h as a unit of power.
- Forgetting to square v in K = ½mv².
- Saying a pendulum is fastest at the extremes.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Numericals (1 mark each): formula, substitution with units, answer with unit.
- Derivations (2–3 marks): start from W = F s; state the equation of motion used.
- Conservation (2 marks): energies at two positions shown equal.

cards.back_md: Energy due to position or configuration.
Energy is neither created nor destroyed; total constant.
Formula, substitution with units, answer with unit.

questions.stem_md: A porter carries a 20 kg suitcase on his head and walks 50 m along a level platform at steady speed. The work he does against gravity on the suitcase is:
questions.solution_md: His upward force is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement: W = F s cos 90° = 0 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A force of 25 N pulls a sledge 4 m along level snow through a rope at 60° to the ground. The work done by the force is:
A book slides across a table and comes to rest. The work done on it by friction is:

options.text_md: positive, because friction acts along the displacement
negative, because friction acts opposite to the displacement
zero, because friction is perpendicular to the motion

questions.stem_md: A satellite moves in a circular orbit round the Earth. The work done on it by the Earth’s gravitational pull in one revolution is:

options.text_md: positive, because gravity pulls it inwards
zero, because the pull is always perpendicular to the satellite’s motion
negative, because gravity slows it down

questions.solution_md: Centripetal force ⟂ velocity at every instant — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A 5 kg bag of rice is lifted from the floor onto a shelf 2 m high. How much work (in J) is done against gravity? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
A gardener pushes a lawn mower with a force of 200 N along its handle, which makes 60° with the ground, and moves it 3 m. Find the work done (in J).

**Assertion (A):** A boy pushing hard against a wall that does not move does no work on the wall.

**Reason (R):** Work is done only when the point of application of a force moves.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Work is a vector quantity because force and displacement are both vectors.
questions.solution_md: False: work is a scalar (product of force, displacement and cos θ).

questions.stem_md: No work is done when the force acts at an angle of ___ degrees to the displacement.
State the formula for work done when a force F acts at an angle θ to the displacement s. Hence explain why a coolie carrying a load on his head along a level road does no work against gravity.

answer.model_answer_md: $W = F s \cos\theta$. His upward force on the load is vertical while the displacement is horizontal, so $\theta = 90^\circ$, $\cos 90^\circ = 0$ and the work against gravity is zero.

questions.solution_md: W = F s cos θ; θ = 90°.

questions.stem_md: An electricity meter shows that a household used 5 kW h in a day. This energy in joules is:
How many ergs are there in 0.5 J?
Which unit is most convenient for the energy of a single electron in an atom?
questions.solution_md: 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, the right size for atoms; horsepower is not even a unit of energy — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A snack bar label lists 2100 J of energy. Express this in calories (1 cal = 4.2 J).
An electric oven uses 7 200 000 J of energy. How many kilowatt hours is this? (1 kW h = 3 600 000 J)

**Assertion (A):** The kilowatt hour is a unit of power.

**Reason (R):** A kilowatt hour is the energy used by a 1 kW appliance in one hour.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: A is false (kW h is a unit of energy); R is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? One joule is equal to ten million ergs.
One electron volt is equal to 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ ___.
Define energy.

answer.model_answer_md: Energy is the capacity (ability) of a body to do work.

questions.stem_md: Convert (a) 1.5 kW h into joules and (b) 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ J into electron volts.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $1.5 \times 3.6 \times 10^{6} = 5.4 \times 10^{6}$ J. (b) Divide by the energy of 1 eV: the ratio of the powers of ten cancels, and $4.8 \div 1.6 = 3$, so the energy is 3 eV.

questions.stem_md: A 60 kg student runs up a staircase 4.5 m high in 9 s. Her power is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
A water pump is rated at 2 hp. Its power in watts is:
Two boys of equal mass climb the same hill, one in 10 minutes and the other in 15 minutes. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: The first does more work and develops more power
Both do the same work; the first develops more power
The second does more work because he takes longer

questions.solution_md: Same mgh, less time → more power — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A motor lifts 500 kg of water to a tank 12 m high in 1 minute. Find its useful power output in watts. (g = 10 m s⁻²)
A 150 W machine does 4500 J of work. How long (in s) does it take?
True or false? One horsepower is equal to 746 watts.
The rate of doing work is called ___.
A power station of 2 GW produces ___ megawatts. (Write a number.)
Distinguish between energy and power, giving the SI unit of each.

answer.model_answer_md: Energy is the capacity to do work (total work that can be done); SI unit joule. Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred; SI unit watt (J s⁻¹).

questions.solution_md: Energy: capacity, J. Power: rate, W.

questions.stem_md: A crane lifts a load of 800 kg through 15 m in 20 s. Calculate (a) the work done against gravity, (b) the power of the crane in kW and (c) its power in hp. (g = 10 m s⁻²; 1 hp = 746 W)
A car’s speed increases from 10 m s⁻¹ to 20 m s⁻¹. Its kinetic energy becomes:
A 3 kg flowerpot rests on a balcony 8 m above the ground. Its gravitational potential energy relative to the ground is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
The kinetic energy of the blades of a spinning ceiling fan, which stays fixed in place, is:
questions.solution_md: The blades turn about an axis without moving along — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Find the kinetic energy, in J, of a 1000 kg car moving at 20 m s⁻¹.
A 2 kg ball has 400 J of kinetic energy. What is its speed in m s⁻¹?

**Assertion (A):** If the speed of a body is doubled, its kinetic energy is doubled.

**Reason (R):** Kinetic energy is directly proportional to the square of the speed.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: A is false (K becomes four times); R is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A stretched rubber band has potential energy because of its configuration.
The energy possessed by a body by virtue of its motion is called ___ energy.
Show that the gravitational potential energy of a body of mass m raised to a height h is mgh.

answer.model_answer_md: To raise the body slowly, an upward force equal to its weight mg must act through the height h. Work done = force × displacement = mg × h. This work is stored in the body as potential energy, so U = mgh.

questions.stem_md: A constant force F acts on a body of mass m initially at rest, and it attains a speed v after moving through a distance s. Derive the expression for its kinetic energy.

answer.model_answer_md: Acceleration $a = F/m$. From $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as$ with $u = 0$: $s = v^{2}/2a$. Work done $W = F \times s = ma \times \dfrac{v^{2}}{2a} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$. This work appears as kinetic energy: $K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$.

questions.solution_md: Using W = F s and v² = 2as.

questions.stem_md: A 0.2 kg stone and a 0.8 kg stone are moving with the same kinetic energy of 10 J. Calculate the speed of each.

answer.model_answer_md: $v = \sqrt{2K/m}$. Light stone: $\sqrt{2 \times 10 \div 0.2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ m s⁻¹. Heavy stone: $\sqrt{2 \times 10 \div 0.8} = \sqrt{25} = 5$ m s⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: In a microphone at a school assembly, the main energy change is:
questions.solution_md: A microphone turns sound vibrations into electrical signals; a loudspeaker does the reverse — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A solar-powered garden lamp charges a battery during the day and lights up at night. The sequence of energy changes is:
questions.solution_md: Solar cell, battery charging, battery discharging, lamp — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? An electric iron converts electrical energy mainly into heat energy.
A dry cell converts ___ energy into electrical energy.
State the energy change in (a) a loudspeaker, (b) a solar cell, (c) an electric heater and (d) a steam engine.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Electrical → sound. (b) Light → electrical. (c) Electrical → heat. (d) Heat → mechanical (kinetic).

questions.stem_md: A coconut falls from a tree 45 m high. Neglecting air resistance, its speed just before hitting the ground is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
A pendulum bob is released from one extreme position. At the mean position its:

options.text_md: potential energy is maximum and kinetic energy is zero
kinetic and potential energy are both maximum
kinetic energy is maximum and potential energy is minimum

questions.solution_md: It is lowest and fastest at the mean position — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A ball is dropped from height H. At what height above the ground are its kinetic and potential energies equal (no air resistance)?
questions.solution_md: U = mgh and K = mg(H − h); equal when h = H/2 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A 3 kg stone is dropped from 25 m. What is its kinetic energy (in J) when it is 10 m above the ground? (g = 10 m s⁻²; no air resistance)
questions.solution_md: Loss of PE $= mg(25 - 10) = 3 \times 10 \times 15 = 450$ J, which equals the kinetic energy.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The amplitude of a pendulum swinging in air slowly decreases.

**Reason (R):** Mechanical energy of the pendulum is slowly converted into heat by air resistance.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The total mechanical energy of a freely falling body is the same at every height.

**Reason (R):** The potential energy of the body is the same at every height.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true; R is false (potential energy decreases as it falls) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Energy can be created in a power station.
questions.solution_md: False: a power station only converts energy from one form to another.

questions.stem_md: At the extreme position of a swinging pendulum, the energy of the bob is wholly ___ energy.
State the principle of conservation of energy.

answer.model_answer_md: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be changed from one form into another, so the total energy of an isolated system remains constant.

questions.stem_md: A 0.5 kg ball is dropped from a window 20 m above the ground. Calculate (a) its potential energy at the window, (b) its kinetic energy just before it lands and (c) its speed just before it lands. (g = 10 m s⁻²; neglect air resistance)

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $U = 0.5 \times 10 \times 20 = 100$ J. (b) By conservation of energy, $K = 100$ J. (c) $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times v^{2} = 100$, so $v = 20$ m s⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: Describe the energy changes during one complete oscillation of a simple pendulum released from an extreme position A, through the mean position B, to the other extreme C and back.

answer.model_answer_md: At A: all potential energy (bob at rest at its highest). A → B: potential energy changes to kinetic; at B all kinetic (fastest). B → C: kinetic changes back to potential; at C all potential. The same changes occur on the way back; the total stays constant (apart from slow loss to air resistance).

questions.stem_md: Match each quantity in Column A with its value in joules in Column B.
questions.solution_md: kW h → 3.6 × 10⁶ J; cal → 4.2 J; erg → 10⁻⁷ J; eV → 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

questions.stem_md: Match each device in Column A with its main energy conversion in Column B.
questions.solution_md: Motor → electrical to mechanical; generator → mechanical to electrical; bulb → electrical to light; cell → chemical to electrical.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define work and state its SI unit. When is the work done by a force (i) zero and (ii) negative? [3]

(b) A trolley is pulled 5 m along a corridor by a force of 40 N applied through a handle at 60° to the floor. Calculate the work done. What would the work be if the same force acted along the floor? [3]

(c) A 45 kg girl climbs a 6 m flight of stairs in 12 s. Calculate (i) the work she does against gravity, (ii) her power, and (iii) her power in hp. (g = 10 m s⁻²; 1 hp = 746 W) [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Work is done when a force moves its point of application; $W = F s \cos\theta$; unit joule. (i) Zero when the displacement is zero or perpendicular to the force. (ii) Negative when the force opposes the displacement (θ = 180°), e.g. friction.

(b) $W = 40 \times 5 \times \cos 60^\circ = 100$ J. Along the floor: $40 \times 5 = 200$ J.

(c) (i) $45 \times 10 \times 6 = 2700$ J. (ii) $2700 \div 12 = 225$ W. (iii) $225 \div 746 \approx 0.3$ hp.

questions.solution_md: Definition and cases; work at an angle; stairs.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define kinetic energy and derive the expression K = ½mv². [3]

(b) A 1200 kg car slows from 25 m s⁻¹ to 15 m s⁻¹. Calculate (i) the initial kinetic energy, (ii) the final kinetic energy and (iii) the work done by the brakes. [3]

(c) Name the forms of kinetic energy, with one example each, and state which form appears in the car example. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Energy of a body due to its motion. A force F accelerates m from rest to v over s: $v^{2} = 2as$, $W = Fs = ma \cdot v^{2}/2a = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$, stored as K.

(b) (i) $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 1200 \times 625 = 375000$ J. (ii) $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 1200 \times 225 = 135000$ J. (iii) Work by brakes $= -(375000 - 135000) = -240000$ J (negative work).

(c) Translational (a moving car), rotational (a spinning wheel or fan), vibrational (atoms in a hot solid, a vibrating string). The car’s energy that is calculated here is translational (its wheels also rotate).

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the principle of conservation of energy. [3]

(b) A 2 kg ball is dropped from a height of 80 m. Calculate its potential energy, kinetic energy and total energy (i) at the top, (ii) after falling 30 m and (iii) just before it reaches the ground. (g = 10 m s⁻²) [3]

(c) (i) Find the speed of the ball just before it lands. (ii) At what height are its kinetic and potential energies equal? (iii) Sketch how U, K and U + K vary with height. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it only changes form, and the total energy of an isolated system remains constant.

(b) (i) $U = 2 \times 10 \times 80 = 1600$ J, $K = 0$, total 1600 J. (ii) At 50 m: $U = 1000$ J, $K = 600$ J, total 1600 J. (iii) $U = 0$, $K = 1600$ J, total 1600 J.

(c) (i) $v = \sqrt{2gH} = \sqrt{1600} = 40$ m s⁻¹. (ii) At 40 m. (iii) U falls linearly with decreasing height, K rises linearly, U + K is a horizontal line at 1600 J.

questions.solution_md: Principle; energies at three points; speed and equal-energy height.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define (i) the joule and (ii) the watt. [3]

(b) Convert (i) 3 kW h into joules, (ii) 4.2 × 10⁵ J into kilocalories (1 cal = 4.2 J) and (iii) 2 hp into kW. [3]

(c) A 1.5 kW heater runs for 4 hours a day for 30 days. (i) Find the energy used in kW h. (ii) Express it in joules. (iii) Find the cost at ₹7 per kW h. (iv) Why is the kW h used on bills rather than the joule? [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) One joule is the work done when a force of 1 N moves its point of application through 1 m in its own direction. (ii) One watt is the power of a device that does 1 J of work per second.

(b) (i) $3 \times 3.6 \times 10^{6} = 1.08 \times 10^{7}$ J. (ii) $4.2 \times 10^{5} \div 4.2 = 10^{5}$ cal $= 100$ kcal. (iii) $2 \times 746 = 1492$ W $= 1.492$ kW.

(c) (i) $1.5 \times 4 \times 30 = 180$ kW h. (ii) $180 \times 3.6 \times 10^{6} = 6.48 \times 10^{8}$ J. (iii) $180 \times 7 =1260$, that is ₹1260. (iv) The joule is too small for household amounts.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is potential energy? Derive U = mgh. [3]

(b) A pendulum bob of mass 0.1 kg is pulled aside so that it rises 5 cm above its lowest point, and released. (i) Find its potential energy at the extreme position. (ii) Find its speed at the mean position. (iii) Where is its speed zero? (g = 10 m s⁻²) [3]

(c) (i) Name the energy changes in a hydroelectric power station. (ii) Why does a swinging pendulum eventually stop? (iii) Is energy lost when it stops? Explain. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Energy possessed by a body because of its position or configuration. Lifting m through h needs an upward force mg acting through h: W = mgh, stored as U = mgh.

(b) (i) $U = 0.1 \times 10 \times 0.05 = 0.05$ J. (ii) $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.1 \times v^{2} = 0.05$, so $v = 1$ m s⁻¹. (iii) At the two extreme positions.

(c) (i) Potential energy of stored water → kinetic energy of falling water → kinetic energy of the turbine → electrical energy. (ii) Air resistance and friction at the support convert its mechanical energy into heat. (iii) No: it is converted into heat (internal energy of the air and support); the total is conserved.
